extra.message: User-controlled parameter 'expr' from query string is passed directly to eval(). While __builtins__ is stripped, an attacker can access builtins through object().__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() or similar techniques to achieve arbitrary code execution. This is a critical remote code execution vulnerability.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code

extra.message: The 'name' parameter from request defaults to 'packet.bin' but can be overridden by the user. It is used directly in BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name without sanitization. An attacker can provide '..' sequences to write files outside the intended directory (path traversal). This allows arbitrary file write on the server filesystem.

The 'packet_ref' parameter defaults to 'dispatch-summary.csv' but is user-controllable. It is used directly in BASE_EXPORT_DIR / packet_ref without any path sanitization. An attacker can use '..' sequences to read arbitrary files from the server filesystem (e.g., etc/passwd, source code, configuration files containing secrets).

The 'url' parameter is user-controllable and passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen(). This allows SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery). An attacker can read internal services, scan the internal network, access cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/), or conduct port scanning from the server.

The 'lane' query parameter is user-controllable (defaults to '/') and passed directly to RedirectResponse. While there is a default '/' value, an attacker can provide any URL including external phishing domains (e.g., ?lane=https://evil.com) leading to open redirect. This can be used for phishing attacks.

The 'card' query parameter is user-controllable and rendered using Jinja2 Template with |safe filter. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the card parameter (e.g., ?card=). Although Jinja2 auto-escapes by default, the |safe filter explicitly disables escaping, making reflected XSS possible.

XML parser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False. User-controlled XML body (via POST) is parsed with DTD and entity expansion enabled. This allows XXE attacks where an attacker can read local files, cause ReDoS via billion laughs, or perform SSRF through external entity references.

The SSRF endpoint at /relay/dispatch-carrier-echo-051 accepts a user-controlled URL and returns the response body to the caller. This allows an authenticated attacker not only to access internal networks but also to exfiltrate the response content, making it useful for reading sensitive data from internal APIs.

SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled using ssl._create_unverified_context() (line 148), and the connection goes to a hardcoded endpoint 'https://partner.invalid/status' (line 147). While this specific endpoint appears harmless in test code, any change to the URL would make the application vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, allowing credential theft or data interception.

The /trace/dispatch-panel-532 endpoint returns internal sensitive information including APP_ENV (environment variable), trace enabled flag, and filesystem path of BASE_EXPORT_DIR. This information can help attackers plan further attacks by revealing the application environment.

The session cookie is set with secure=False (line 269), meaning it will be sent over unencrypted HTTP connections. An attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack can intercept and steal the session token. Additionally, samesite is set to 'lax' which provides weaker CSRF protection than 'strict'.

cwe: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in Session Cookie Without 'Secure' Attribute

extra.message: The seed script uses a hardcoded demo password 'Password123!' for all test accounts (admin, dispatcher, customer, workers). This password is also echoed in the seed output JSON (line 229-242), making it visible to anyone with access to database seed data or initialization output.

CORS allows all origins with allow_methods=['*'] and allow_headers=['*'] combined with allow_credentials=True. While the origin list is limited in this configuration, if an attacker-controlled origin were ever passed through (e.g., via a misconfiguration), credentials would be sent to any origin. Additionally, /ops/* endpoints in dispatch_operations.py echo back the Origin header directly as CORS header (line 91-92), allowing arbitrary origins when accessed.

cwe: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

extra.message: MongoDB connection is established with user-controlled payload (request.json) passed directly as the find_one query filter. An attacker can inject {$gt:''} type comparisons or other MongoDB query operators to bypass filters or extract data. While not XXE, this represents NoSQL injection risk from user input.

The /frame/dispatch-slip-482 endpoint explicitly disables security headers: X-XSS-Protection is set to '0' and Content-Security-Policy is empty string. This removes browser-level XSS protections and could allow browsers to render potentially malicious content without restriction.

The export/incidents endpoint (lines 860-863) exports internal_notes field in CSV for any user with visibility into incidents. While role checks exist, the internal_notes are operational data that should not be included in mass export without additional access controls on individual fields.

The session cookie uses samesite='lax' which allows cross-site POST requests and GET on top-level navigation. For a session management cookie, 'strict' is more appropriate to prevent CSRF through cross-site requests.

The /spool/dispatch-fan-308 endpoint accepts a 'count' parameter (default 500) with no maximum validation. An attacker could set count to an extremely large value (e.g., 10**9), causing excessive memory allocation and potential denial of service through resource exhaustion.

The seed script prints the demo password and all account credentials to stdout (lines 228-242). Anyone with access to process output, logs, or terminal will see these credentials in plain text. This is a critical issue for deployment scripts that might capture stdout.

cwe: CWE-532: Exposure of Log File to Unauthorized Persons

extra.message: The webhook test endpoint at /api/admin/webhooks/{webhook_id}/test returns the full webhook payload including the URL in the JSON response (line 919). While this is admin-only, webhooks could be configured to point to attacker-controlled URLs, and an admin triggering a test would send requests to those URLs with whatever authentication the webhook has.

The Docker Compose file contains a hardcoded database password 'dispatch' for the PostgreSQL service (lines 7-8). This is a default credential that could be used by attackers if the docker-compose.yml file is leaked or deployed to production without modification.

The SECRET_KEY for JWT signing falls back to 'local-dev-change-me' when the environment variable is not set (line 14). If an application is deployed without setting this, all JWT tokens can be forged by anyone who knows this default key, completely breaking authentication.

The password reset confirm endpoint (lines 328-338) has no rate limiting. An attacker can brute-force password reset tokens by making many requests. While the token is a secure random value, if there are timing vulnerabilities or weak token generation, this could be exploited.

cwe: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits

extra.message: The list_webhooks endpoint (lines 876-883) returns the full webhook URL in plain text to ops_admin users. While this is admin-only, any sensitive credentials embedded in webhook URLs (e.g., http://user:pass@host/webhook) would be exposed.

The MongoDB connection uses MONGO_URL from environment variable which is not validated. If an attacker controls the environment (e.g., through a separate vulnerability), they could inject arbitrary connection strings to redirect database queries to an external server, exfiltrating data.

The /origin/dispatch-mirror-472 endpoint reads the Origin header from the request and sets it directly as the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header (lines 91-92). This makes the CORS configuration dynamic and user-controlled, bypassing any server-wide CORS policy. An attacker can craft a malicious page at evil.com that sends a request to this endpoint, and the server will respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: evil.com, allowing the attacker's JavaScript to read the response.

cwe: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains
